protocol: RE-RANKING, not open retrieval. For each seed, only that seed's labelled candidates are ordered. No retrieval is issued and nothing is embedded, so corpus coverage of unlabelled documents is irrelevant to the measure — which is what makes this admissible where an open-retrieval evaluation on 33.6% coverage would not be.
why_not_open_retrieval: Under open retrieval a relevant article the corpus does not hold cannot be returned at any rank, so the score is capped by coverage and reports corpus size. See relish-feasibility.json.

configurations.similarity_only: cosine similarity between stored embeddings; characterises the encoder
configurations.deployed_ranker: similarity + 0.1*lexical + 0.08*citation + 0.04*recency, replicating PgVectorService exactly; characterises what a searcher receives

deployed_constants.lexical_normalisation: pool-relative: text_rank divided by the maximum text_rank among that seed's candidates, which is the faithful translation of the service's MAX(text_rank) OVER ()
deployed_constants.lexical_query_form: plainto_tsquery, conjunctive — an AND over every lexeme of the query text

gain_schemes.map: binary, only the top label counts as relevant, which is the convention LitSense 2.0 states for its MAP
gain_schemes.average_precision_when_no_relevant_in_to: ZERO, not undefined. Eligibility guarantees every seed has at least one relevant candidate somewhere in its list, so a top-n containing none of them is a ranking failure rather than an absent measurement. Treating it as undefined would exclude exactly the seeds where the ranking did worst: on MAP@5 that was 47 of 1,209 seeds and it lifted the figure from 0.835 to 0.869. LitSense 2.0 does not state its convention for this case, so their MAP column may not use the same one, and that is a further reason their figures and these are not comparable cell for cell.

lexical_term_behaviour.note: Measured rather than assumed. plainto_tsquery is conjunctive, so using a whole abstract as the query builds an AND over every lexeme in it, which essentially no candidate satisfies. A lexical term that is zero for this structural reason is a different claim from one that is zero by accident, and the counts here establish which it is.

map_convention_finding.what: The MAP column of the published comparison almost certainly counts PARTIAL as relevant, while the figures reported above count only the top label, which is the rule that source states.
map_convention_finding.how_established: MedCPT is the encoder LitSense 2.0 ranks with and its weights are public, so it was run through this same harness on these same 1,209 seeds. Its nDCG@10 came out at 0.7958 against the 0.7658 their paper reports — a gap of 0.030. Its MAP@10 came out at 0.7393 against their 0.9147 — a gap of 0.175, for the identical model on the identical benchmark. A difference in subset difficulty cannot be small on one measure and large on another for one model. Recomputing MedCPT's MAP with partial counted as relevant gave 0.9219, a gap of 0.007. See medcpt-relish-scored.json, map_convention_probe.
map_convention_finding.consequence: Setting the strict MAP figures above beside that source's MAP figures compares two different quantities, and the apparent deficit is an artefact of that. The strict figures stay as the reported ones because the strict rule is what the source states; the lenient block exists so the comparison can also be made under the convention the evidence supports.
map_convention_finding.caveat: This is an inference from one model at one cutoff, not a statement the source makes about itself. It is strong enough to stop the strict-versus-their-MAP comparison being presented as meaningful, and not strong enough to assert their exact definition.

litsense_published_for_reference.note: From LitSense 2.0, Nucleic Acids Res. 53:W361-W368 (2025), Table 2, on THEIR unpublished test split of RELISH. NOT comparable cell-for-cell with the figures above: a different subset, a different split, and their pipeline re-ranks a lexically retrieved candidate set. These figures were read from their paper; LitSense was NOT re-run on the seeds evaluated here, because its public API exposes search over its own index and not pairwise scoring of a supplied candidate list. Recorded so a reader can see the order of magnitude, not so a winner can be declared.

disclosures: This is NOT a head-to-head. LitSense 2.0 reports on the test portion of RELISH and that split is not published with their paper, so the subsets differ and no cell can be compared directly. Their figures here are quoted from their paper, not re-measured.

The retained subset is not a random sample of RELISH. It is the part this corpus happens to hold, and the corpus is topic-scoped and requires an abstract, so the retained pairs may be systematically easier or harder than those excluded. That is not correctable by restriction.

Seeds are retained only if the seed and at least five candidates are held and at least one retained candidate is labelled relevant. A seed whose relevant candidates were all excluded would otherwise score zero for a reason that is coverage, not ranking.

RELISH is an article-to-article similarity task, so the query is a stored abstract rather than a composed question. That is the verbatim-text condition this evaluation reports separately elsewhere, and it is the easier condition for any system.

RELISH labels TOPICAL relevance only. The citation prior exists to prefer well-established work, which is a different property, so it may cost score here while still serving a searcher. The paired comparison reports the direction either way.
